entities.name: Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī, a pivotal figure in early Islamic science, was an Arab philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer who flourished in Baghdad during the nascent Abbasid Caliphate, dying around 806 CE. His significance lies primarily in his role as a conduit for the transmission of Indian scientific knowledge into the Islamic world, laying foundational elements for the flourishing intellectual movement known as the Translation Movement. Working under the patronage of Caliph al-Manṣūr and later Hārūn al-Rashīd, al-Fazārī was instrumental in integrating foreign sciences, particularly from India, into the burgeoning Arabic scholarly tradition.

Al-Fazārī's most notable contribution was his involvement in the translation and adaptation of the Indian astronomical treatise, the *Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta* by Brahmagupta, which arrived in Baghdad around 771 CE. This work, often referred to in Arabic sources as the *Sindhind*, introduced the Islamic world to advanced Indian mathematical and astronomical concepts, including the use of Hindu-Arabic numerals and sophisticated trigonometric tables. Al-Fazārī, possibly collaborating with Yaʿqūb ibn Ṭāriq, produced an Arabic version of the *Sindhind*, which became a cornerstone for subsequent Islamic astronomical tables (*zījes*). He is also credited with constructing early astrolabes in the Islamic world, potentially the first Muslim scholar to do so, demonstrating a practical application of theoretical astronomical knowledge.

entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī (born c. 746 CE, Kufa; died c. 806 CE) was a pivotal Arab polymath whose work at the dawn of the Abbasid Golden Age fundamentally shaped Islamic scientific tradition, particularly in astronomy and instrument-making. Operating under the patronage of Caliph al-Manṣūr and later Hārūn al-Rashīd, al-Fazārī was instrumental in transmitting and synthesizing sophisticated Indian and Hellenistic astronomical knowledge into the nascent Islamic intellectual sphere, thereby laying critical groundwork for centuries of scientific advancement.

His most significant contributions include the construction of the first astrolabe in the Islamic world, a complex instrument vital for celestial navigation and timekeeping, and his pivotal role in translating the Sanskrit astronomical treatise *Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta* by Brahmagupta. This translation, known as *Kitāb al-Sindhind al-Kabīr*, was a watershed moment, introducing sophisticated Indian mathematical and astronomical concepts, including positional notation and the use of zero, to the Islamic world. He also authored several astronomical tables (zijes) that synthesized these diverse traditions, further integrating them into Abbasid scholarly practice.

Al-Fazārī's work had profound and lasting consequences, effectively establishing the foundational curriculum and methodology for Islamic astronomy. The *Sindhind* became the most influential astronomical text in the Islamic world for over a century, directly impacting subsequent scholars like al-Khwārizmī, whose own zijes were built upon al-Fazārī's translations and interpretations. His pioneering efforts in instrument design spurred the development of a rich tradition of Islamic scientific instrumentation, making Baghdad a global center for astronomical observation and innovation.
